questions.q: Ryan changed a customer's address offline, but meanwhile the server's copy has changed. What should happen?
questions.hint: Write it anyway, or tell someone?

options.text: The server keeps whatever arrived last and says nothing
options.why: That is last-write-wins; Kevin's change is silently lost.

options.text: The server doesn't write without matching the base version, returns 409, and both copies are shown
options.why: The conflict is caught, nobody loses anything, and there is a chance to reconcile.

options.text: When Ryan's phone returns, it overwrites its own change with the server's full copy
options.why: That loses Ryan's work. The work of both sides has to be saved.

questions.q: The client sent the same change twice (the first reply was lost). What does the server need so that no harm is done?
questions.hint: How would the server know it has seen this change before?

options.text: A mutation id for each change, and a list of applied ones
options.why: On seeing the same id a second time, the server says "duplicate" and does nothing.

options.text: The timestamp of the change
options.why: A device timestamp can't identify duplicates reliably, and it tells you nothing about whether the change was applied.

options.text: Forcing the client to send only once
options.why: When the connection drops, the client can't know whether the first send succeeded.

questions.q: In which case will field-level merge work correctly?
questions.hint: Did the changes land in the same field?

options.text: One person changed the address, the other the phone number
options.why: Different fields, so both changes can be kept.

options.text: Both changed the title, each in their own way
options.why: A same-field conflict; merging doesn't settle it and the user has to choose.

options.text: One deleted the record, the other edited it
options.why: This is also a real conflict, so automatic merging isn't safe.

questions.q: What problems does this code have?
questions.hint: What happens when the tab closes, and when the server returns 409?

options.text: The outbox lives only in memory, so offline changes are lost when the tab closes
options.why: Without IndexedDB, it isn't really local-first.

options.text: A 409 isn't told apart from other failures, so a conflict just sits there
options.why: When `res.ok` is false the change stays in pending and the user is told nothing.

options.text: Using `JSON.stringify` is wrong
options.why: It is fine; JSON is the normal way here.

options.text: `fetch` can't be used offline, so it will never work
options.why: Offline, fetch fails, and catching that failure and keeping the change in the outbox is the standard approach.

questions.q: Two people are changing stock counts offline. Which approach is safest?
questions.hint: Is the change a "total" or an "add and subtract"?

options.text: Send a new total each time and keep the last one
options.why: If the two totals differ, one person's work is lost and the count is wrong.

options.text: Send changes like "+2 cartons" and "-1 carton", and the server adds them up
options.why: Additions and subtractions give the same total in any order. That is the idea behind a CRDT counter.

options.text: Let only one person edit offline
options.why: It ruins usability, and the problem returns anyway once that person comes back online.

questions.q: Ryan edited one note twice offline, both edits with base v5. The server accepted edit 1 and replied "version 6". What should the phone do with edit 2?
questions.hint: Edit 2 was written on top of edit 1. Where does the phone get the true version number?

options.text: Send it as it is, with base v5
options.why: The note is v6 now, so the server answers 409 and Ryan conflicts with himself.

options.text: Set its base version to 6, the number the server returned, then send it
options.why: Edit 2 is now written against the version that already contains edit 1, so it matches and goes through.

options.text: Have the phone guess base + 1 for edit 2 at the moment Ryan writes it, offline
options.why: If Kevin also changed the note meanwhile, the guess hides the conflict and silently overwrites Kevin.

options.text: Throw edit 2 away, since the server already has a newer version
options.why: That loses Ryan's work; the edit was fine, only its base version was out of date.

questions.q: On an order-tracking page, you want to tell the user the moment the status changes. Which is the best fit?
questions.hint: Which way do the messages flow?

options.text: Poll every second
options.why: With thousands of users it is hugely wasteful, and it still delays by up to a second.

options.text: SSE, with Symfony Mercure
options.why: One-way news, plain HTTP, and the browser reconnects by itself.

options.text: WebSocket, because it is the most modern
options.why: No frequent messages go from the browser here, so WebSocket's extra complexity is pointless.

questions.q: Which of these statements are correct?
questions.hint: Think about what each technology was made for.

options.text: SSE goes only from server to client
options.why: To send from browser to server you use an ordinary POST.

options.text: With WebSocket, messages go both ways
options.why: Over the same connection, client and server can both send at any time.

options.text: EventSource never reconnects once the connection drops
options.why: The browser reconnects by itself and sends Last-Event-ID.

options.text: In long-polling the server never holds the reply
options.why: Holding is the whole trick: the reply is held until something new arrives.

questions.q: What is wrong with this Vue code?
questions.hint: What happens to the connection after the user leaves the page? And what if the topic is private?

options.text: There is no source.close() on unmount, so connections keep piling up
options.why: The `source` variable also lives inside onMounted, so there is no way to close it from outside.

options.text: For a private topic, `withCredentials: true` is missing, so the browser won't send the cookie
options.why: To send the cookie to a hub on another origin you need `withCredentials`, or authorization fails.

options.text: The current state isn't fetched when the stream opens, so the user misses changes made before connecting
options.why: A live stream brings only changes made after it opens. Fetch the true state with a plain GET on every open.

options.text: You can't use `JSON.parse`
options.why: e.data is a string, so JSON.parse is exactly right.

questions.q: The user has the phone app closed and the order arrives. How do you tell them?

options.text: Send it over the SSE connection
options.why: The app is closed, so there is no open connection at all.

options.text: Send a push notification (FCM/Web Push), and fetch the status from the server when the app opens
options.why: The OS push channel arrives without a connection, and the current state should come from the server.

options.text: Poll every second
options.why: With the app closed, there is nobody to poll.

questions.q: What is the problem with holding SSE connections in PHP-FPM, and what is the fix?
questions.hint: What does each open connection tie up?

options.text: Each connection ties up an FPM worker; keep the connections in a separate hub (Mercure)
options.why: The number of workers is limited, so with thousands of connections even ordinary requests get stuck.

options.text: No problem, PHP-FPM holds thousands of connections easily
options.why: In FPM each request takes one worker, so open connections use up the workers fast.

options.text: Just adding more RAM fixes it
options.why: The limit is the number of workers; more RAM only raises cost while the structural problem remains.

questions.q: An app has 1 million users, most with fewer than 200 followers, and the feed is opened 100 times more often than posts are written. What is the best starting choice?

options.text: Write-time fan-out
options.why: Followers are few and reads dominate, so 200 writes at write time are cheap and every feed read is fast.

options.text: Read-time fan-out, with a JOIN every time
options.why: Running a heavy JOIN on every frequent read makes the database buckle.

options.text: No feed; just show all posts by time
options.why: That doesn't separate the posts of the people the user follows. There is no feed anymore.

questions.q: A celebrity has 5 million followers. What happens when they post under write-time fan-out?
questions.hint: How many feeds must one post be written to?

options.text: 5 million writes are created, the queue fills up, and everyone else's posts are delayed
options.why: This is the hot key problem: one user slows the whole system.

options.text: Nothing happens, Redis handles it all
options.why: Redis is fast, but 5 million writes and the load on workers and the queue are still there.

options.text: Only the celebrity's own feed is updated
options.why: The post is placed in the followers' feeds, not in the celebrity's own.

questions.q: Which of these statements about hybrid fan-out are correct?
questions.hint: Which posts are spread, and when?

options.text: An ordinary user's post is placed in followers' feeds at write time
options.why: Followers are few, so spreading is cheap and reads stay fast.

options.text: A celebrity's post is fetched and merged when the feed is read
options.why: It avoids millions of writes, and fetching a few celebrities' posts is cheap.

options.text: Every post runs read-time first and write-time after
options.why: There is no such rule; the split is based on the user's follower count.

options.text: A copy of a celebrity's post is stored in every follower's feed
options.why: This is exactly what hybrid avoids.

questions.q: This handler ran twice because of redelivery. What happens to the feed?
questions.hint: What happens when you add the same member to a sorted set again?

options.text: The post will appear twice in every feed
options.why: Members in a sorted set are unique. Adding the same postId again creates no new row.

options.text: Nothing changes, because it is the same member with the same score
options.why: `ZADD` is idempotent. Running it a second time gives the same result.

options.text: An exception is thrown the second time
options.why: Redis ZADD throws no exception; if the member exists, it just updates the score.

questions.q: What goes wrong if you show a feed's "next page" with `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20`?
questions.hint: What happens if a new post arrives while the page is open?

options.text: New posts push earlier posts onto the next page again
options.why: When a new post enters at the front, every row shifts back one place, so the last post of the previous page appears again.

options.text: With a large OFFSET the query gets slow
options.why: The database has to walk past every row up to the OFFSET.

options.text: Nothing is wrong, this is the best way for feeds
options.why: In a feed where new data keeps arriving, OFFSET is especially unreliable.

options.text: OFFSET doesn't work in feeds at all
options.why: It works, but with the problems above.

questions.q: A page holds 2 posts. Posts 9, 8 and 7 share one millisecond. The cursor is the time alone, "older than this". What does the reader see?
questions.hint: Which posts count as "older than" a time they share?

options.text: Page 1 shows 9 and 8; post 7 is never shown
options.why: Post 7 has the same time as the cursor, so it is not older and is skipped. The cursor must also hold the id.

options.text: Page 2 shows post 7 first, as expected
options.why: It would only if the cursor said "same time with a smaller id", which a time-only cursor cannot say.

options.text: Posts 9 and 8 appear again on page 2
options.why: Those are not older than the cursor either. The problem is a post missing, not one repeating.
